To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human GRP xenografted shiverer mice show extensive migration of grafted cells, but not myelination, and that this is sufficient to significantly extend lifespan.
human GRP xenografted shiverers survive for more than 50% of the animals for over 50 weeks while mouse GRPs allografted shiverers do not extend survival beyond 20 weeks.
human glial‐restricted progenitor transplantation can rescue the survival in dysmyelinating mice, independent of the production and maturation of myelin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a cell therapy for dysmyelinating disorders.
the use of stem cells as a treatment for diseases of the central nervous systems (CNS) that involve dysmyelination, such as leukodystrophies.
the development of new therapies to treat diseases of the central nervous systems, such as multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“Transplanted human GRPs can rescue the survival dysmyelinated animals independent of the production and presence of mature myelinated fibers”.
the therapeutic effect of glia‐restricted progenitor cell (G‐RPC) transplantation is dependent on migration of the cells and not the production of mature and compacted myelin.

the therapeutic effect of GRPs in dysmyelinating diseases is independent of the production and presence of compact myelin, and is instead mediated by the extensive migration and integration of transplanted cells into host tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human glial‐restricted progenitor cell transplantation can extend survival of dysmyelinative disease independent of the production or maturation of myelin.

the therapeutic outcome of GRP transplantation is dependent on the presence of human cells and their extensive migration, but independent of the presence of mature mylenin, suggesting that the therapeutic effect of GRPs is not solely attributed to myelin production.
the therapeutic outcome of human GRP xenografted shiverers is dependent on the ability of human GRP to migrate and extend lifespan of the host, and that this is independent of myelinating potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the production of mature mylin is not required for a therapeutic effect of glia transplantation in dysmyelinating diseases, and that the extent of cell survival and migration are more critical for the therapeutic outcome.
the therapeutic effects of glial‐restricted progenitor transplantation in dysmyelinating diseases may not depend solely on the formation of mature and compacted myelin.
transplanted glial‐restricted progenitors can extend the survival in dysmyelinating shiverer mice independent of the presence of mature myelinating myelin sheath.
